fixes.explanation: That's right, friend. Ezekiel, a priest (Ezekiel 1:3), says, "…the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet…" He had just fallen facedown before the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28). I think a boost like that was welcome.

Yes, and the LORD says it plainly: "To this very day they and their fathers have rebelled against Me." The fathers are in it too, not just the people standing in front of Ezekiel. He's walking into a long story.

Close, but the LORD names more people than that. He says, "To this very day they and their fathers have rebelled against Me." The fathers are in it too, not only the ones living now. So it's not only them.

The LORD doesn't point at a few kings here. He says, "…they and their fathers…" and He calls the whole thing a rebellious nation. The rebelling reaches "To this very day…" and includes the fathers. It's a bigger crowd than one palace.

Right. The LORD never promises easy. He says, "Do not be afraid of their words or dismayed by their presence, though they are a rebellious house." The word is "though," so the rough crowd stays in the picture. Ezekiel is told not to fear them.
Nothing about robes or dust here. The LORD's next words are, "Open your mouth and eat what I give you." Ezekiel's next job is dinner, and nobody gets to be sad on an empty stomach.
Yes, baker. The words on the front and back are "…lamentation, mourning, and woe." That's a lot of ink on both sides, and none of it light reading. Hold onto that, because the taste comes up next.

That would be a nicer scroll, friend, but it's not this one. The text says the words were "…lamentation, mourning, and woe." And they're written on the front and back, so flipping it over won't get you a cheerier page.
That's it. Ezekiel says, "So I opened my mouth, and He fed me the scroll." He opens his mouth, just as the LORD told him to.

Yes. The LORD says, "…the house of Israel will be unwilling to listen to you, since they are unwilling to listen to Me." The reason He gives is their unwillingness to listen to Him. They're turning away from the One who sent Ezekiel.

The text gives a different reason. The LORD says they "…are unwilling to listen to Me." Ezekiel is sent to "your people, the exiles" (Ezekiel 3:11), but the LORD never says they find him a stranger. The reason He gives is about their unwillingness to listen to Him.

Hands and feet aren't on the list, friend. The LORD says, "…I will make your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads." He later adds, "I will make your forehead like a diamond, harder than flint" (Ezekiel 3:9). So it's the forehead getting the diamond treatment, not the feet.

Yes. Ezekiel says it was "…the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another and the sound of the wheels beside them, a great rumbling sound." Those living creatures were part of the vision that dropped him facedown (Ezekiel 1:28). I think that's a rumble he won't forget.

Close on the voices, but not the source. Ezekiel says it was "…the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another and the sound of the wheels beside them, a great rumbling sound." The exiles don't come into it until he reaches Tel-abib (Ezekiel 3:15).

That's right. Ezekiel says, "…I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD upon me." The text doesn't say why he felt that way. It does say the strong hand of the LORD was upon him.

Yes. Ezekiel says that for seven days he "…sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed." The text doesn't say why he was overwhelmed. I think after the scroll and that rumble, it was a lot to take in.
